English translation:
(Docket) [Registered] by Flavius Victor, most glorious comes and patricius, most distinguished, through Dorotheus, most glorious stratelates and tabularius, [...] 9th indiction. (Main text) In the reign and consulship of our most divine master Flavius Iustinus, the eternal Augustus and Imperator, year five, on the nineteenth of the month Hathyr of the present fourth indiction, in the most splendid city of Antinoe. I, Flavius Phoebammon, son of Euprepius of blessed memory, the late chief physician, originating from this beautiful city of the Antinoites, subscribing below in my own hand, make and set up the present just and lawful testamentary will, as a last written disposition, unsealed and without seal impressions because of the weakened poverty of our modest station and the very small, rather scanty and bare extent of our property, so that my heirs may, whenever they wish, make its force manifest and know indisputably and without contest what it contains, both in its chief part and in its simple wording, once and for all, in the following terms. Death is the end of all things and of the mortal race, and it is wholly impossible to escape it; but for those of sound mind to foresee it and take precautions is the most fortunate of all things. I therefore, the aforenamed Phoebammon son of Euprepius, chief physician, having of necessity considered my own situation, have resolved to dispose of all my affairs before death as is fitting, with right and good conscience, just intent and exact reckoning, while I am among the living, in accordance with what is granted by the divine laws to all who are of sound mind, with all freedom, power and authority to dispose (of their goods) to their own dear children, and not to leave them disputes after death. In this way, while I live, am in good health, walk in the market place doing my usual business, with sober reasoning, just intent, good conscience, exact thought and firm disposition, I have come to this written testamentary will, understanding, thinking, keeping my reasoning and mind unimpaired, and having, as I said, my body healthy, by the kindness of the all-powerful master of all things, God almighty, taking care lest I suddenly depart from the affairs here intestate, before I have first disposed and arranged all my very small affairs, both those I have in the countryside in various places, inherited from my parents and acquired myself, and those in this city of Antinoe and in every place. In accordance with what is divinely granted to all mortals to do while they live, I have drawn up the present testamentary will, as I said, civil and praetorian, in the presence of the seven lawful witnesses summoned at my request, citizens, adult Romans, of good repute, who also subscribe it below in one meeting and at one time, with no other act intervening, in accordance with the force of the laws; this testament I dictated in Greek words and ordered it to be written in Greek letters in a public and business place. And I wish it to have its own strength and force in all the chapters it contains, according to the distinction of each, and to hold no less the rank of a codicil and of every last will and fideicommissary letter, being produced and published before every authority, power, throne and lordship at every time and occasion, according to what is divinely ordained by the laws, and all the chapters in it to be given and fulfilled against those who wish to inherit my rights on intestacy; further that these things to be determined by me shall alone proceed intact and be kept unshaken for my most beloved legitimate sons and them alone, for whom I justly and reasonably make the following dispositions. But if after this I make a codicil or codicils and dispose other chapters in them, I wish it or them also to have their own force and confirmation as confirmed in the present last will. May it be granted me to live for some further time, as it may please God, the mightier and master, and to enjoy my modest station likewise and all my very small property: it shall be permitted me by the laws, as long as I survive, to hold possession of all my goods with just and usual ownership and the usufruct of all my property, that is the whole ususfructus, after the pious public dues, both regular and occasional, on them. But when I suffer some human fate and depart from the affairs here by the necessity of destiny, then I appoint as heirs my most beloved sons and successors to my inheritance and all my property, in the countryside in various places and in this city of the Antinoites and in every place, so that they, with all authority and power, after my death, shall hold, own and be masters of all my goods, both those inherited from my parents and those I acquired, which came to me by whatever just and lawful written title and means, and inherit them without hindrance or impediment from anyone at all, and without complaint, of necessity; and further that they rightly inherit, as I said, all my goods of every kind which I shall leave, in equal share, per capita portion corresponding equally, of movables, immovables and self-moving things, every obligation and action, in every form, kind, material, quality and quantity, from the costly kind to the cheap, of wood, earthenware and glass, down to one assarion, obol and lepton, simply every receipt and payment on my behalf; and if I justly owe anything or, so to speak, am owed anything, they shall pay these and receive (what is owed) undiminished again in equal shares. I wish my aforementioned sons and heirs to inherit all my goods as I said, except what I dispose and determine below in my present testamentary will. I wish then and order that the pious and all-venerable monastery called that of Apa Hieremias of holy memory, likewise after my death, shall receive at once, with all authority and power, one clean aroura of fruitful vineyard land in full, of sixty-four hammata, measured by the public cord, of land free of and not subject to taxes, separated from the whole vineyard properties which came to me from the succession and inheritance of my father of blessed memory Euprepius, chief physician, lying at the village of Ibion Esembythis of the Hermopolite nome, under the watch of the same (village), to its east, according to the neighbouring holdings, from whatever place and corner of the same vineyards it wishes, four-square all round, with everything belonging to the aforesaid one aroura of fruitful vineyard land, of water-supplies, dwellings and all equipment, farmsteads, chaff-stores, water-wheels and fitted wooden machines and all their extent in general, not previously subject to any claim, burden or pretext or any occasion whatsoever, but clean throughout, eternal and unfailing, to belong to the aforesaid monastery with every guarantee and clearance, for an eternal memorial and intercession, for the propitiation of my soul and holy offering, when I depart to God. For I grant this aforesaid one aroura planted with vines as an irrevocable favour and lawful written gift to the aforesaid pious monastery, for the healing of my soul, having this force unalterable and an unrepented intention, in whatever manner, ground, time and place, but sufficiently holding every secure form and that inter vivos according to the law, so that it may never suffer any overturning before any authority, power, throne and lordship under the sun, since I gave it as a favour and a gift with good and sincere intent to the aforesaid pious monastery for my eternal holy offering. And I determine that its royal tax shall always be drawn, charged and returned upon all my property, being taken up continuously with the whole public tax owed to be given on my behalf by my sons and heirs, both regular and occasional, in wheat of the embole, gold tax, freight and all burdens, (my heirs) answering forever for it to the public account and satisfying it for it continuously, and freedom from disturbance, sedition, demand, loss, distraint and molestation being always kept for the pious monastery, in return for which I gave it to it for the rest of my soul and the remission of my sins, on condition that the abbots, stewards and administrators of the affairs of the same holy monastery at any time, and then also the present administrator and superior and God-loving father Apa Besas, the most reverend presbyter and head of the community, shall by right of ownership, according to every right of property fitting by the laws, become masters of the same one vineyard, as I indicated, and collect all its revenue each year from the crops and dues of the coming (year), with God, and of that year and of the following time forever and completely, and arrange its administration as they wish for my holy offering; yet they shall never be able to alienate it or exchange it with another for all time, but it shall be permanent and enduring, serving my holy offering, because this has so rightly and justly been resolved by me. I wish and order my dear sons to make the laying-out, that is the funeral, of my body according to my rank, and I adjure the reverend and God-loving abbot of the aforesaid monastery of Apa Hieremias, by the consubstantial, holy and unconquered Trinity, to receive my remains for burial and a tomb in the most pious monastery, for the remembrance of my lowliness always, and that my name be counted in the list of all the blessed who rest there, in the expression of the enerad(n)oumion(?). I wish and order my most noble consort and wife to have power over her own and only the wedding gifts given her by me at the time of her auspicious marriage before intercourse, and to be content with these and not be able to seek anything beyond them from any heir or co-heir of mine, nor to take authority in any way to carry off any thing at all of all my goods, as is likely if she should wish to appropriate any of my goods with ill intent and profit from them; may this not happen to her after my death; but she shall be permitted only to take her own parental goods when she leaves my house, which shall be shown with proof to have been brought in to me by her from her parents. I determine in all respects the holy administration, care and forethought of our pious hostel according to the paternal traditions, and I wish and order that all the care and attention and provision of diet for the sick be carried out carefully, laboriously and without neglect, practised with piety and fear of God, with all zeal and fairness, and that it be performed by my most beloved brother Iohannes, and that he shall likewise have the care of the affairs of the same hostel, as is fitting, for the complete renewal of the attention to, service and maintenance of the sick as usual; and I adjure him by the everlasting God not to be slack in this most zealous work of God; and if he neglects it, he will answer to God. I ask and beseech all the faithful and merciful, and also the distinguished and most learned advocates, whom I also adjure by the Holy Trinity, and every judge, magistrate, authority and lordship, always to keep this my testament in force, without any opposition, contrariness, reasoning of rhetors or decanal hair-splitting. For all who belong to me and are related to me by birth I declare, not in insult, to be [cast off], without share and without lot altogether, and I wish and order that they be kept far from my share in everything, inheritance and holding of goods, as bastards and freedmen, being estranged from all these in every respect, and from every receipt and payment on my behalf, because I have judged with right and just intent and chosen so. For each one should enjoy his own; and the very few goods of my modest station will hardly suffice for my infant and under-age sons, to whom I shall leave a gloomy and unmanaged life, needing much upbringing, many expenses and care. And, as I have determined, I wish all my goods to be assigned and to belong to them alone, and I fix a penalty of one pound of gold, to be paid, against anyone who shall wish impiously to do them harm, and (I wish) that with this he shall in no way benefit [from the] attempt, but rather be harmed and [defeated], and unwillingly and without profit keep quiet about what has [now] been disposed by me in this my just testament, [from which] let all envy and wicked guile be absent. And may it be [secure], directed by Jesus our Lord and God and [always kept] in all the [general chapters] it contains; approving these I have also set down this [chapter], which, to put it briefly, is evidently [more valid] and more secure than almost all of these, as I [think], and should likewise proceed by command: that my said dear sons and heirs shall be protected, given a curator and fittingly managed, with their very small goods, as infants and under age, until [they grow] in age, by my master and God-loving father Apa Besas, the superior of the aforesaid pious monastery [of Apa] Hieremias, as general curator and guardian according to the laws. And I ask him and adjure him by the face of God almighty and his honoured and surpassing salvation, insofar as he has acted fairly and zealously in every good work pleasing to God, to take upon himself this soul-profiting (task) too, in piety towards God and love of mankind, and to take care fittingly, carefully and laboriously of my said wretched children and their very small goods until, as I said, their lawful age, so that they are not unjustly defrauded by any person as orphans and without protection, as they are not and will not be able to call him, the said (curator), to account in any respect; and (I ask them), at my request, [to respect] the most God-loving curator [and] to obey him in all things as (they would) me. [And having] good [hope], I trust that he will not neglect to do [all that ...] serving [...], and therefore I order them [to listen to and present] to him the help and care of them, through [piety and] fear of God, and that he will not set them aside, for [his own salvation]; but if he neglects, which be far from him, their administration, may he be [answerable] at the fearful tribunal of God, [giving] account to the almighty God and father of orphans for this [negligence]; but if he takes good care of them, may God himself, the giver of plenty, in return for these labours reward him with a rich hand from those unspeakable good things [of his] with recompense ten-thousandfold, and make him long-lived, until he comes to the enjoyment of all his hope and [salvation]. For I, the wretched one, shall go the way of all, needing the propitiation [and] intercession of all, and I [no] longer find (how) to give him thanks for these things. My aunt, by name [...], I ask and wish to seek out, whence she knows, the ... silver, lying with the moneylender, which I pledged to him by way of pawn and by right of mortgage [for whatever its value is, and to divide] these and sell them to whoever wishes, and at the same time [to keep] its price, and first to pay off to the [said] creditor out of it the loan, then to [take the surplus and] appropriate to herself the excess of the price, [on account of her] maintenance for the whole time of her life, [yet she shall] never [be able] to claim any other thing [against my heirs], nor they [to raise a claim] against her [about this in any] manner, ground, time [and place, but to abide by what has been determined], because each party [has thus ... receiv]ed the inheritance (?) fitting to it in full [...]. I wish and order and again give to the aforesaid holy monastery of Apa Hieremias, through the most God-loving Apa Besas, the aforesaid abbot, and those who will succeed him in the abbacy of the place, my new boat of my two equipped boats, with all its equipment as it is, and the written deed of former purchase by which it came to me by right of purchase from some Antaeopolites, from whom, although I have it, I hold the sale (deed) which I now wish to be handed over to the same place, to be under all its authority, for continuous, complete and eternal possession, ownership, use and collection of its revenue, as is fitting, likewise for the remission of my sins before God and for the healing of my soul. Since I justly owe the most distinguished lord Christophorus son of Theodorus fifty solidi, of full weight [and plain], on the standard of Antinoe, I likewise ask the God-loving abbot Apa Besas to receive these from Petrus, the most admirable receiver, out of [what] is owed to me by him for my customary [annonae], that is the sixty solidi, in accordance with the judicial order [received] by me, for the present fourth indiction, and to pay them back to him (Christophorus) and take back for cancellation the [pledge] which he holds for them. I wish and order that there be [given], out of piety, to Athanasius who is being brought up by me, on the [Epiphany] each year, by way of legacy, out of my very small property, [until] his lawful age only, ten artabas of wheat and four [of barley], twelve xestai of oil, twenty jars of wine. [But after he] reaches the same full age, as I said, [I then wish] the aforesaid legacy to be cut off and cancelled [and] to return to me, that is to my heirs, as an [acquisition], undivided. And on these terms and on all that has been [disposed] and determined by me, I have set down and disposed the present testamentary will with all exactness as a [written] will, valid and secure, in the reign and consulship of our most divine master Flavius Iustinus, the [eternal Augustus] and Imperator, year five, on the [nine]teenth of the present month Hathyr, of the present fourth indiction, in [the most splendid city] of Antinoe.

In the reign of our most divine and most pious master Flavius Iustinus, the eternal Augustus, [greatest benefactor and Imperator, and of Aelia Sophia our most pious mistress, year ...], Pachon .., 6th indiction. Flavia Christodote, with God, illustris, daughter of Iohannes of glorious memory, former patricius, to you, Flavius Eustathius, most distinguished comes and banker. I give formal notice concerning the matters set out below. Good faith in transactions, when kept, sets those who made them in praise and preserves unimpaired the disposition of those who came to an agreement, just as its contrary, when trampled on, clearly brings about the opposite. Your magnificence remembers, then, how you guaranteed to me in writing, concerning my most glorious brother the lord Cometes, sixty-one pounds of gold with the interest accruing on them within a stated term; and behold, the term has passed and you have not satisfied your guarantee, so that I have now been made ready to go to the queen of cities and obtain my rights through the fortunate and just reign; for I now have (recourse) against no one but your splendour, which undertook to me, on behalf of my said most glorious brother, the guarantee of the same sixty-one pounds of gold, in many (words?). For that I struggle with many debts and am troubled every hour by the moneylenders is plain to all; moreover the immovable property left to me in the Arcadian (nome), from which I have my necessary maintenance, is about to be handed over by force of circumstance to the moneylenders, so that the loss resulting from this falls upon your splendour, which has not until now furnished me what is owed to me by it, so that I might free myself from my moneylenders. Whether, then, any loss is inflicted on me for this reason, or I run a risk regarding the immovable property left to me in the Oxyrhynchite, or I incur expenses on account of travel abroad, I shall demand these from your splendour, which does not bear to satisfy me without trouble according to its guarantee. For the removal of every excuse, and so that your splendour may know that through its delay it becomes liable to me both for the expenses incurred by me, as is likely, through your postponement, and for what will be taken from my property by my moneylenders because I cannot give what I owe, since I have not received from your splendour what was guaranteed to me by it on behalf of my most glorious brother: I have therefore used the present protest, sent to it through the most learned ekdikos of Alexandria, with my subscription and that of his learnedness, a copy of which I have kept with me for my own security, with the endorsement of the said most learned ekdikos. And I swear by the holy and consubstantial Trinity and the victory and permanence of our most victorious masters Flavius Iustinus, the eternal Augustus, greatest benefactor and Imperator, and Aelia Sophia our most pious mistress, not to leave Alexandria unless it (your splendour) first satisfies me for the gold guaranteed to me by it, as has been said.

In the consulship of Flavius Theodoric, vir clarissimus, Phaophi [..], in the seventh indiction, in the village of Coba [of the Heracleopolite nome]. Flavia Carteria alias Cyrapanton, daughter of Ausonius of pious memory, formerly presbyter [...], to Flavius [...], devoted stratelatianus, my full brother, [...] the same most pious [...], greeting. I acknowledge by this written security of mine that I have received from you, in various ornaments [...] of (your) wife [...], set with stones of various hyacinths and pearls (?), valued at thirteen [gold solidi], and a chalaston (an ornament), also valued at twenty gold solidi, and [one] pair of bracelets, valued at four gold solidi; total 37 gold solidi. These I have received from you on account of the bond for the thirty-five solidi; and since this same bond has been lost and has nowhere been found, I acknowledge that it is void and invalid whenever it is found and produced by anyone [...] in court and out of court, [because] I have been paid by you the [same thirty-]five solidi on account of the same bond formerly made by you; [and I have no claim] against you concerning this, nor (have) my heirs, successors or assigns [...] [...] in court and out of court. The acknowledgement is valid wherever it is produced; and having been asked I have agreed and released [you as stated above. I, Flavia] Carteria daughter of Au[sonius ...]. English translation:
[... in the name of the holy Tr]inity, consubstantial [...] [... in the mo]nth Hathyr 6 of the year [...] 9th indiction. [I, Paham, the m]onk, son of Epiphanius [...] [of Psenanto]nios, which is in the nome of the city of Keft (Coptos), [...] with my whole heart and my whole will, without [...], there being no compulsion upon me, nor deceit nor robbery, [but by] my own will and my free choice, without fear, with good [counsel and] without disturbance, my mind being sound, my reasoning firm, my heart [set]tled [...], with my whole heart and my free choice, without fear, to write for you, you my [son Ja]cob, my beloved, to write for you a firm and indissoluble writing, a [testament] for ever, for you and your children and your children's children and all your heirs who will obey [you] according to your word. I, Paham, wrote this testament with my own hand, dwelling on the mountain of Jeme, being a monk. They saw that there is no one according to the flesh who has stayed with me in that place; I considered that man does not know his way; I said: lest a sickness come upon me and I die suddenly, there being no one with me to whom I may declare my word about the few trifling things that I have from my father and my mother, and their dwellings. Since [... I had thr]ee sons; I went and became a monk; I left them alive; they lived in the world, the three. Concerning the eldest son, Papnoute: he took a wife against my will; I was very, very grieved, but he who ... did not know (it)(?) from the time he took her; many quarrels and disturbances happened in his affairs; they came south to me and told the matter to me, that her virginity was not intact(?); I said that I have no business with him, because he disobeyed me; I left the matter to God, the true judge, and to the prayers of my holy father. After he went from me they deceived his mind with words of flattery; they left her to him; he begot children with her, his heart being grieved about it; and he used to come and tell his grief to me many times and make my heart more grieved; but I did not wish to cast him out, for God's sake, because they are my bowels(?); I gave him a little place to dwell in, in my house, with his furnishings, whether silver or gold or bronze or clothing; in short, what I gave him is noted, written in another place. After this God visited him like every man; he died with his children at one time; he left no seed alive to him now. As God made him a stranger to this world with his children, I also make him a stranger to all my dwellings which came to me from my parents and his wife(?), and to my inheritance which I have now; no person acting for him shall take any of them. Concerning the house which I gave him to dwell in until he died: his wife shall not be able to inherit it and dwell in it as its owner, nor any person acting for her, but Jacob shall take it from her and inherit it with his children for ever and ever. Concerning the furnishings which I gave him, Papnoute, while he was alive: when he died I searched for them; I found that he had lost none of them down to (the least) item while he lived, but I found that he owed two solidi and a half. Behold, now I give you the authority, you, Jacob, my son whom I love, my beloved, and you are master to search for every item that I gave to Papnoute and that he himself acquired, down to a single item, valuable or poor. After this you shall pay his creditor the two and a half solidi, and you are master to make his wife swear in every oath-place you wish over an item of (even) a potsherd, because I am the one who commands as long as I live. After this, also, he gave me the authority, through those who sat with him at the time he was dying: his wife shall swear concerning what she brought in to him and take it, apart from the share(?). You too, Jacob, do for her as for the widows who are around you in your village, being childless, and let her go to her house with ... and to her village from which she came. Concerning Thatre, my daughter: I have separated her share in every matter, being master of it, according to what God put into my heart, whether what is mine from my parents or from her mother, so that there is no claim with Jacob her brother concerning any item from today on, by me, Paham her father; but if someone comes against them on account of their mother, Jacob and Thatre shall divide it between them: a third part to Jacob, a third to Thatre, and the other third part they shall give as an agape for the soul of the deceased, that is Papnoute and Susanna his mother and Martyria the mother of Susanna. If after my death you, Jacob and Thatre, find occasion to claim with your sisters'(?) ... your mother Susanna, that is Iohannes and the persons of her husband(?) who died, and they say 'your mother and your father took their share, we settled with them while they were alive', behold, I place here the holy oath, swearing by God the Almighty, ... that when Susanna your sister came against me, I Paham, she never brought anything in to me openly(?) ... in my thoughts, whether her parents gave it to her for her need or she took it by theft and brought it in to me. Concerning the items which we divided among us, I Paham and Gera and Iohannes and his partner(?): we put some at my disposal and my share at the time we divided; but we agreed, I Paham and Gera, that Sibla should swear an oath to us concerning the rest of the items. Concerning the gold over which they went to law: they gave us none of it at all, I Paham and Gera, but Iohannes and Sibla took it. After this, at any time you wish to claim against them concerning the gold and the rest of the items, you are the ones who command according to your wish. Behold, I have fulfilled them with the oath of the Lord, lest they make excuses saying 'we settled with your father while he was alive'. I, Paham, am the one who first wrote the ... in my own hand, having written the testament with my hand alone, writing to Jacob my son: concerning the site of the house which came to me from Epiphanius the presbyter, his(?) father, because he is the one who built it, and it came to me, I, the son of Epiphanius the presbyter: behold, I too give it to you alone and your children to inherit, with those who come after you who obey you; no person shall be able to come against you ever, whether son or daughter or grandchild, concerning that house which lies west of the hagios Collouthus: its one wall on the street of Apa Collouthus, the other is the vault(?) which takes its boundary at the house of the blind man, the other wall up(?) the street towards the door inward; concerning the other wall to the south: the house of the herdsman(?) Samuel and the house of Abraham son of Touba. I have named the names of the old documents which are in those houses for the sake of the present day. Concerning the wall which Isaac built by violence, because we had no freedom of speech at that time, being on the mountain(?): perhaps when God gives you a way you will build it ... seek out builders; they will inform you whose the wall is ... and our fathers never left it to be added to; not only this wall, but all the others around the house. Concerning the furnishings(?) inside, the place of ... it shall be wholly yours to its boundaries; if you wish to build it, you are master in every matter of what is yours. Concerning the third part of the houses which I ... for my mother in the south in the village of Thyre, and the third part of my furnishings in that place, which came to Thatre my mother from Sara her mother: behold, I Paham give them to you, Jacob my son; no person shall be able to claim against you for them ever. Concerning Thatre, my daughter and your sister: you shall not be able to cast her out from the place in which she is living, all her days, lest her son take a wife and her heart not be at rest with her and she come and live in it, because man does not know what will befall him. When she dies, whether you are alive or dead, she shall not be able to order, saying 'give it to my son' or 'to whom I wish'; if she says so, she shall be a stranger to God; and whoever is great at that time who supports her in doing this, he too shall be a stranger to God; because I saw my father treat his sister in this way until he died, and none of them(?) lived in it as strangers ... according to her need, so that no neglect occur; you shall not hinder her from living in what is yours alone, but you shall not let any stranger live in it. I did this so that no one ... to that place. I, Paham, write to Jacob that in every matter, whatever came to me from my parents, whether house or furnishings or any vessel, from the valuable to the cheap, they shall all be yours and your children's and those who come after you, as one law(?). No person shall be able to claim against you for any matter [...] what I did not write, or what I did not think to write, or what I did not remember to write; but all these I am master of as long as I live, I, Paham, the least. I said: lest, while I live, I fall into sickness and you neglect me; if you do my will in my life, you shall inherit everything that is mine after my death. Behold, then, I have drawn up the testament of my hand, firm for you and those after you; and any person who comes against you over the testament wishing to claim against you, whether kin or kin of kin, or a person whom we do not remember, whoever comes against it shall be a stranger to the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit and the perfect Trinity which we worship at all times. The testament shall be firm and shall not be dissolved, for this is how it pleased me, and I wished and drew it up according to what God put into my heart, with my own hand, dwelling on the mountain of Jeme at the time I drew up the testament. Whether I am alive or after I have laid down the body according to the lot of every man, whoever shall come against you, Jacob, over the testament, wishing to dissolve it, whether brother or sister or brother's wife or heir or any person at all, shall be a stranger to the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit and every communion of Christians, and after this he shall pay a great fine to the archon who rules at that time, according to what God puts into the heart of that archon, because they wished at all to take counsel in their heart to dissolve this testament on which the name of God is written and the fearful oath which we have placed upon it. And the bishop at that time, if he wishes to neglect and destroy the testament, or says at all that it is not firm, wishing to dissolve it, whether through words of flattery or through foolish people or through gifts, and any person in the order of priesthood, whether bishop or presbyter or deacon or reader or layman, who wishes to dissolve the testament, shall be a stranger to the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, and he shall come and be judged with me at the fearful tribunal of God. After this also the archon who rules at that time, or pronoetes or lashane of the village, or any person at all who helps a person dissolving the testament, shall be a stranger to the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, the consubstantial and life-giving. I, Paham, have drawn up this testament with my own hand, firmly, and it shall be valid in every place where it is produced. I, Theophane, son of the blessed Iohannake, man of the city of Kos(?), Apa(?) Paham asked me; I am witness to the testament at his request. I, Abernoukios, the least presbyter of the catholic (church) of Psinai, am witness to this testament at the request of Apa Paham the monk. I, Kyrillos, son of the blessed Phoibammon the hegoumenos, am witness. I, Isaak, son of the blessed Phoibammon, in Psinai, am witness. I, Philotheos, ... in Pishenai, am witness to the testament as it is written. I, Paham, the least monk, son of Epiphanius, presbyter of the hagios Collouthus of Psenantonios, I, Paham, wrote the testament with my own hand and I agree to everything written in it; and after this I asked other trustworthy people; they witnessed it; and whoever shall dissolve my command shall be a stranger to every communion of Christians.

English translation:
[I, brother Kalimach]e, the monk of the monastery of the holy Apa Apollo, [write to my brother] [...] [the mon]k of this same monastery: since [...] you took a solidus for me, I [will give it at the harvest of] this year of the eleventh indiction. [Now, then, by the wil]l of God I am [ready to give] what came ... at the harvest. I swear [by God the Almigh]ty that I will observe and keep (it) [according to the force of this secur]ity, as it is written. [...] [I, ...], am witness. [I, ...], am witness. (Verso) The security of Kalim[ache] [...].
